Foot Of Altitude

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Slide a point along the bottom of a triangle and watch the short line between the places where its two lines meet the sides; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag a corner or the sliding point, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show names, right angles or the circle, and press Reset to start again.

Drag A, B, C or D; with the keyboard, focus a point and press arrow keys (Shift moves further).

Look for the math

A point slides along the bottom of a triangle. Two short lines drop from it to the other sides, and their ends mark a segment whose length changes. The surprise is that the same simple spot makes it shortest for every triangle — even when that spot lies outside the bottom side.

The shortest place for D

The answer is the foot of the altitude from A to the line BC. Call it D′; let E′ and F′ be its projections on AC and AB. The applet draws E′F′ as the green bar and the length at the current D as the violet bar. The logic test compared the bar lengths at thousands of triangles and sliding positions, including obtuse ones: EF at D′ was never larger than at any other point of the base line. The applet fixes B, C and D to a horizontal line, so D may slide past B or C; when the foot is outside the side, it is still the minimum on that line. The page notes that Honsberger's exception for an obtuse base angle (where he puts the minimum at the vertex) is incorrect; the test agrees for the applet's line.

A circle with AD as its diameter

Because DE is perpendicular to AC and DF to AB, the angles AED and AFD are right angles. So A, E, D and F lie on one cyclic quadrilateral, and AD is a diameter of its circle. The chord EF subtends the angle EDF at D; by the inscribed angle rule this angle is the same as the angle at A, or its supplement, whichever way the points turn. The test found that EDF stays fixed (up to that supplement) as D slides; at the instant D reaches B or C one of the lines has zero length, so the angle is undefined there.

Minimizing without calculus

A chord of a fixed circle that subtends a fixed angle has length diameter × sin(angle), which the page also gets from the law of sines:

EF = AD · sin(∠EDF)

The sine factor does not change as D moves, so EF is shortest exactly when AD is. The nearest point of a line to A is its perpendicular foot, giving E′F′ ≤ EF without calculus. When angle A is a right angle, AEDF is a rectangle: the sine is 1, AD and EF are its equal diagonals, and the test confirmed EF = AD for right triangles with D in several places. On the page this last calculation is Gordon Walsh's solution; the words here follow the page, and the check script verifies the identity over every triangle in its sample.

Try the circle box and slide D slowly past the foot: the circle shrinks with AD, and the violet bar reaches the green bar exactly at the foot.
